title: Voting propensity and parental depression

selected_claim.evidence_location: Results section, Table 1 (full-sample model for voting propensity at age 26); Measures section for exposure and outcome definitions.
selected_claim.evidence_summary: In the full-sample age-26 linear probability model, parental psychological distress was associated with a 0.171 lower probability of intending to vote (β = −0.171, p < 0.01), adjusted for the listed covariates. This is an adjusted observational association, not proof of a causal effect.
selected_claim.x: Mean parental Malaise Inventory score across when the cohort member was age 5 and age 10 (a 0–24 measure of parental psychological distress).
selected_claim.y: Voting propensity at age 26: a binary indicator of whether the cohort member said they would vote if there were a general election tomorrow.
selected_claim.target_population: Members of the 1970 British Cohort Study included in the full-sample age-26 analysis (Table 1 reports N = 5,253).
selected_claim.adjustment_description: The full-sample age-26 linear probability model adjusts for the cohort member's psychological distress and childhood/family background, cognitive ability, and adult sociodemographic characteristics.

article_review.evidence: In the full-sample age-26 linear probability model, parental psychological distress was associated with a 0.171 lower probability of intending to vote (β = −0.171, p < 0.01), adjusted for the listed covariates. This is an adjusted observational association, not proof of a causal effect.
article_review.evidence_location: Results section, Table 1 (full-sample model for voting propensity at age 26); Measures section for exposure and outcome definitions.
article_review.adjustment: The full-sample age-26 linear probability model adjusts for the cohort member's psychological distress and childhood/family background, cognitive ability, and adult sociodemographic characteristics.

evidence_summary: The focal paper examines whether mean parental Malaise Inventory psychological-distress scores at cohort-member ages 5 and 10 are associated with the cohort member's stated propensity to vote in a hypothetical general election at age 26. Its full-sample age-26 linear probability model (Table 1, N=5,253) adjusts for cohort-member psychological distress, childhood/family background, cognitive ability, and adult sociodemographic characteristics. The provided claim does not report an effect estimate or direction, so none is asserted here.
x_definition: Parental depressive symptoms or psychological distress, measured as the mean parental Malaise Inventory score across the cohort member's ages 5 and 10.
y_definition: Electoral turnout propensity: whether a person would vote or abstain, including stated intention or probability of voting in an election.

splits.description: Depressive symptoms or psychological distress: symptom severity, experiences, or screening measures of depression or nonspecific psychological distress in a person, including measures of a parent or caregiver.
Judgments about willingness or conditions to forgive a person or group for perceived transgression.
Intentions, willingness, motivation, duty, or readiness specifically for voting and electoral participation.
Traits and relatively stable dispositions associated with the UOA's own distress, such as neuroticism, negative affectivity, rumination, and emotional regulation difficulties.
Exposure, eligibility, or direct effects of electoral laws, rules, policies, and programs governing voting rights, access, registration, procedures, or incentives.
Intentions, motivation, civic duty, efficacy, or readiness to participate in civic or political action, including voting-related participation.
Personality measures specifically capturing aggression or aggressive disposition, distinct from other broad personality and self-related dispositions.

category-moral-values-judgment.reason: The evidence on the exposure link concerns an interpersonal standard for forgiving someone who has committed a transgression; the evidence on the outcome link concerns the importance assigned to civic duty. These are distinct moral domains, and the findings do not establish that one common moral-values construct links parental distress to turnout.
category-moral-values-judgment.exposure_examples: The distress-side finding concerns requiring transgressors to perform acts of contrition before forgiveness, an interpersonal moral judgment about responding to wrongdoing. It reports a link with psychological distress among older adults.
category-moral-values-judgment.outcome_examples: The turnout-side finding concerns perceiving civic duty as important and links that norm to a person’s decision whether to vote.
category-moral-values-judgment.why_not_confounder: The findings do not show that the same underlying moral value affects both parental depressive symptoms or psychological distress and turnout. An interpersonal forgiveness standard is not interchangeable with a civic-duty norm, so their separate associations cannot by themselves support one common confounder inference.
category-moral-values-judgment.new_group_rationale: A group focused on civic duty or moral obligation to vote would coherently capture the outcome-side finding because the measured norm is specifically about civic participation and is linked to voting.
category-moral-values-judgment.residual_group_rationale: The residual group would cover interpersonal moral judgments about forgiveness and contrition, which are coherent around evaluating wrongdoing and conditions for forgiving, and are linked here to psychological distress rather than turnout.
category-moral-values-judgment.boundary_cases: General moral conviction could overlap both domains, but the cited findings do not measure such a shared construct. A judgment that a particular transgression is wrong or that contrition is required fits the residual interpersonal group; a belief that voting is a civic obligation fits the civic-duty group. Broader, nonspecific moral values remain uncertain without evidence linking the same measure to both distress and turnout.

The retained findings support links between genetic variation or liability and depressive symptoms, and between genetic variation and voting turnout. In the intergenerational setting, parental genetic liability could contribute to parental distress while inherited variants could affect the cohort member's turnout. The evidence does not establish this specific parent-to-offspring pathway, but the genetic concept is coherent across both links.

The findings concern apprehension about disease or health threats on both links: health concerns are associated with depressive symptoms or psychological distress, and perceived health threats are associated with turnout. confounders.reason: The main-specification design feature c16 restricts the analysis to the age-26 sample. This directly absorbs variation in life stage and broad chronological age across the age-26 analysis; the cohort was born in the same week, so there is also little birth-cohort variation. It does not absorb any small differences in exact age at interview within the wave. This is a design restriction, not an age covariate.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the exposure was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

Entry c1 (Age Mother Completed Education / parental education completed) is a direct pre-treatment control for parental educational attainment and appears in the age-26 model. It may not capture the cohort member’s own educational attainment or participation. Entry c10 (Age left education) also relates to education, but the inventory classifies it as an intervening variable, so it does not count as a confounder control.

No pre-treatment control or design feature in the inventory covers transient or situation-specific emotion/affect. c8 (cohort members’ distress) measures offspring mental-health symptoms and is an intervening variable, not a proxy for transient affect; in any case, an intervening variable does not count as confounder adjustment. The other inventory entries do not match this concept.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

The age-26 focal model includes social class at birth (inventory entry c6), a direct measure of family-of-origin social position, and also parental education (c1) and parents’ marital status at birth (c5), which capture additional family-background dimensions. These controls address some socioeconomic and family-structure aspects of the broad confounder, but do not capture all parental characteristics or childhood experiences, such as parental voting, parenting practices, or adversity. I do not count tenure (c4), because the inventory classifies it as an intervening variable.

The pre-treatment control c5, parents’ marital status at the cohort member’s birth, appears in the age-26 model and directly controls one component of family structure. It may not capture later family transitions or household composition, so control is incomplete for the broader group. Cohort members’ adult marital status (c12) is an intervening variable and does not count as confounder adjustment.

Entry c3, Mother's age at delivery, is a pre-treatment control included in the full-sample age-26 model in Table 1. It is a proxy for the timing of childbearing, but does not capture other fertility or reproductive behaviors such as parity, pregnancy intentions, or infertility.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

The age-26 full-sample model includes gender as a pre-treatment control: Table 1 adjusts for whether the cohort member was allocated male or female at birth. This directly controls the inventory concept, though the binary sex measure may not capture gender identity or other gender-related variation.

No control-inventory entry covers genetic variants, genotype, or polygenic propensity, and no listed design feature absorbs genetic variation. The paper adjusts for childhood and family background and offspring distress, but none is a genetic control; offspring distress is also an intervening variable, not a pre-treatment control for this confounder.

No control-inventory entry covers subjective identification with, attachment to, or internalization of a social group, occupation, team, organization, or role. The listed education, socioeconomic, demographic, and offspring-distress controls do not measure or reasonably proxy group identification.

No control-inventory entry covers health concerns or serves as a reasonable proxy for them. c8 (cohort members’ distress) measures offspring symptoms rather than health concerns, and its intervening_variable role means it does not count as confounder adjustment. The other listed controls do not measure or proxy health concerns.

The focal age-26 model includes social class at birth (inventory entry c6) as a pre-treatment proxy for the socioeconomic and material-resource dimension of housing and living conditions. Social class can track typical differences in access to housing and living standards, but it does not directly measure tenure, crowding, housing security, or dwelling quality. The more direct matches—tenure (c4) and persons per room (c2)—are designated intervening variables and therefore do not count as confounder controls.

The age-26 focal model includes social class at birth (c6), a pre-treatment proxy for the cohort member’s adult income through the persistence of socioeconomic position across generations. It may not capture the cohort member’s actual earnings, income changes, or current household income. Employment status (c11) also relates to economic resources, but the inventory classifies it as an intervening variable, so it does not count as a control.

No control inventory entry covers information or communication exposure or a substantively reasonable proxy for it. The listed pre-treatment controls address parental education, maternal age, family structure and social class, and gender; none tracks respondents' information exposure. The closely named distress, education, and employment entries are intervening variables, not confounder controls. No design feature absorbs variation in information exposure.

No control-inventory entry covers interpersonal or social trust, and none of the listed controls is a reasonable proxy for it. The paper therefore does not adjust for this confounder in the age-26 model.

The only inventory match is c11 (cohort members’ employment status), a direct measure of employment and labor-market position included in Table 1. However, c11 is classified as an intervening_variable, so it does not count as adjustment for this confounder; no pre-treatment control or design feature addresses labor-force status. The paper’s social-class-at-birth measure is not a sufficient proxy for labor-force status, particularly unemployment or labor-force entry and exit.

No control inventory entry covers geographic residence, region, or urbanicity, and none is a reasonable proxy for location. Tenure (c4) is an intervening variable and describes housing tenure rather than geographic location, so it does not count as a control. The sample restriction (c16) and full- or balanced-sample designs (c13, c14) do not absorb geographic variation.

No control-inventory entry measures or absorbs objective aggregate economic conditions such as unemployment, inflation, recession, inequality, or local economic shocks. c6 (social class at birth) and c1 (parental education) are pre-treatment controls for the family's socioeconomic position, but they do not proxy the surrounding aggregate economic context. The other potentially related entries, including c2 (household crowding) and c4 (tenure), are intervening variables and therefore do not count as confounder controls; the sample restrictions do not absorb contextual economic variation.

No inventory entry directly controls or reasonably proxies migration/citizenship status or history. The design entries restrict the sample or address changes in sample composition; they do not absorb migration-related variation. The listed matching entries concern different concepts, and the inventory classifies several as intervening variables rather than pre-treatment controls.

No pre-treatment control or design feature in the shared inventory covers moral values or moral judgment. The listed family-background controls do not measure this concept, and cohort members’ distress (c8) is an intervening variable, not a control for moral judgment.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No control-inventory entry covers peer-group norms or a substantively reasonable proxy for them. The model adjusts for family background, cognitive ability, and adult sociodemographic characteristics, but these do not control for peers’ norms or behavior.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No pre_treatment_control or design_feature in the inventory directly controls or substantively proxies the broad group of stable personality dispositions. c7 (Childhood Cognitive Ability) is the nearest conceptual overlap for cognitive-style aspects, but it is an intervening_variable and measures ability rather than personality broadly; it therefore cannot count as a control. The other listed controls do not capture this confounder.

No inventory entry controls physical functioning or disability, or provides a reasonable proxy for it. c11 is employment status, not a typical-respondent proxy for physical functioning, and its role is intervening_variable in any case; c8 measures offspring distress rather than functioning and is also an intervening_variable. The other controls and design features do not absorb physical-functioning variation.

No control-inventory entry covers direct exposure or eligibility for a law, program, institutional rule, or policy treatment. The listed socioeconomic and family-background controls do not adjust for policy exposure itself; no matching design feature absorbs it. Therefore this confounder is unaddressed.

No control-inventory entry covers prosocial orientation, charitable behavior, volunteering, or helping. The listed childhood and adult socioeconomic controls are not substantively reasonable proxies for prosocial behavior. The design features do not absorb its variation, so it is unaddressed.

No inventory entry directly controls race/ethnicity/origin or reasonably proxies it. c6 controls parental social class and economic position, which may correlate with racial or ethnic background but does not track that background for typical respondents. c9 controls sex assigned at birth, not race/ethnicity/origin. The c16 complete-data sample restriction does not absorb variation in race/ethnicity/origin. Thus the age-26 specification does not address this confounder.

No control-inventory entry covers religion or a substantively reasonable proxy for religious affiliation, belief, religiosity, or practice. The model includes childhood and family background and adult sociodemographic controls, but none adjusts for religion. Cohort members’ distress (c8) is an intervening variable concerning offspring mental health, not a control for religion.

No inventory entry controls for social interaction or serves as a reasonable proxy for the broad concept of interpersonal contact and social networks. c5 adjusts for parents’ relationship status at birth, but that does not capture social interaction generally. c12 covers adult partnership status but is an intervening_variable, not a pre-treatment control, and partnership status alone would not represent broader social contact or support.

No eligible inventory entry controls the UOA’s social status. c6 (social class at birth) is the closest pre-treatment control, but it measures the parents’ occupation-defined class, not the UOA’s perceived or objective rank; occupation-defined social class is also excluded by this unit’s definition. c1 (parental education) is not a reliable proxy for the UOA’s status. c4 (tenure), c10 (age left education), and c11 (employment status) could relate to material position or adult socioeconomic position, but they are designated intervening variables and therefore do not count as controls. No other listed control or design feature addresses status.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No inventory entry covers actual technology or digital-service use. The listed pre-treatment controls do not measure or reasonably proxy it; entries for cohort-member distress, education, and employment are intervening variables, not controls for this confounder. The design features restrict or characterize the sample but do not absorb technology-use variation.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No inventory entry is a pre-treatment control or design feature that covers the cohort member’s personal or current household accumulated wealth, assets, or debt. c6 (social class at birth) concerns childhood family social position and does not proxy the cohort member’s current wealth. Although c4 (tenure) and c11 (employment status) relate to resources, both are classified as intervening variables and therefore do not count as controls under the inventory rules.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the outcome was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.

No control inventory entry covers or reasonably proxies job or workplace attributes such as demands, autonomy, schedules, climate, and employment conditions. c11 (employment status) is not a proxy for these attributes: status does not track the variation in job conditions among workers, and the inventory classifies it as an intervening_variable, not a pre-treatment control. The work-characteristics confounder therefore remains unaddressed.

No pre-treatment control in the inventory directly measures or reasonably proxies distress-associated personality and self-regulation traits. The nearest entries are c8 (cohort members' distress) and c7 (childhood cognitive ability), but both are intervening variables, not controls; moreover, they measure symptoms and cognitive ability rather than stable traits such as rumination, neuroticism, or emotion regulation. Under the inventory rules, neither counts as adjustment for this confounder.

No supported confounding path: every finding on this confounder's link to the exposure was excluded, so it cannot confound the focal relationship. This status was set from the findings alone; the paper's specification was not reviewed for it.
